coaches.title: The Vanishing Line
coaches.focus: Main claim, paragraph roles, and careful transfer
prompts: Give each paragraph a short job label. Which paragraph changes or qualifies the argument?
Write the author’s main claim in one sentence, including its qualification.
Identify one piece of passage evidence that should rule out an overly broad answer.
hints: Separate a view the author describes from the position the author defends. Look for a shift in stance.
Compare the final claim with the paragraph beginning a qualification. Keep both in your summary.

model.label: Paragraph 1
model.text: Introduce the inherited hierarchy and its historical contingency.

model.label: Paragraph 2
model.text: Test and reject function as a fixed dividing rule.

model.label: Paragraph 3
model.text: Consider intention and attention; relocate the distinction to the beholder.

model.label: Paragraph 4
model.text: State the cultural-judgment thesis and its responsibility for inclusion.

model.label: Paragraph 5
model.text: Qualify: judgments can be reasoned even though the boundary is not natural.

model.label: Main claim
model.text: Art and craft are separated by revisable cultural judgments, not an intrinsic border in objects.

model.label: Boundary
model.text: A culturally drawn boundary can still answer to skill and tradition; the author does not say all objects are equally valuable.

model.label: Transfer example
model.text: An everyday object entering a museum changes the context of attention, without acquiring a new physical essence.

model.label: Paragraph 1
model.text: Question the assumption that fidelity is a single fixed property.

model.label: Paragraph 2
model.text: Contrast literal meaning with poetic effects as competing standards.

model.label: Paragraph 3
model.text: Explain translation as interpretation and choice.

model.label: Paragraph 4
model.text: Qualify: defensible interpretation still excludes misreading.

model.label: Paragraph 5
model.text: Show that translation resolves ambiguities left open in the original.

model.label: Paragraph 6
model.text: Recast responsible choice as a condition of translation.

model.label: Main claim
model.text: Translation necessarily chooses among competing forms of fidelity; those choices should be textually defensible.

model.label: Boundary
model.text: Plural standards do not license any interpretation whatsoever.

model.label: Transfer example
model.text: Two adaptations can make different defensible choices, but neither can ignore evidence that contradicts its reading.

coaches.title: Titrating an Unknown Weak Acid
coaches.focus: Design, evidence, and the limit of a claim
prompts: State the research question. Name what changed, what was measured, and what was held constant.
Select the data comparison that matters. Describe its direction before calculating.
State one conclusion and one thing this design cannot establish.
hints: Treat each column as a variable with units. Identify which comparisons isolate the proposed factor.
A result supports a claim only within this design. Ask whether a control or an additional experiment would remove an alternative explanation.

model.label: Question
model.text: Does the titration behavior support a weak monoprotic acid, and what is its pKa?

model.label: Changed
model.text: Volume of 0.100 M NaOH added to the acid.

model.label: Measured
model.text: Equilibrated pH after each addition.

model.label: Comparison
model.text: The deionized-water titration provides a comparison without acid buffering. Temperature, acid aliquot, and titrant concentration are controlled.

model.label: Evidence
model.text: At half-equivalence, 12.50 mL, pH is 4.74, so pKa is approximately 4.74. Equivalence near 25 mL has a basic pH.

model.label: Limit
model.text: Sparse sampled volumes cannot locate the exact point of maximum slope; calibration, mixing, and the monoprotic-acid assumption affect interpretation.

model.label: Question
model.text: Does compound X change ALP kinetics in a manner consistent with competitive inhibition?

model.label: Changed
model.text: Substrate concentration and absence or presence of 100 micromolar compound X.

model.label: Measured
model.text: Initial product-formation velocity in nmol/min.

model.label: Comparison
model.text: Buffer-only reactions at each substrate concentration; enzyme amount, pH, temperature, and ionic strength are matched.

model.label: Evidence
model.text: X lowers measured velocity at each tested substrate concentration. The passage describes the same extrapolated Vmax and a higher apparent Km with X, consistent with competition.

model.label: Limit
model.text: The largest measured substrate concentration is not infinity. Table points alone do not prove equal asymptotes or directly demonstrate binding at the active site.

coaches.title: Knocking Down HSF1
coaches.focus: Design, evidence, and the limit of a claim
prompts: State the research question. Name what changed, what was measured, and what was held constant.
Select the data comparison that matters. Describe its direction before calculating.
State one conclusion and one thing this design cannot establish.
hints: Treat each column as a variable with units. Identify which comparisons isolate the proposed factor.
A result supports a claim only within this design. Ask whether a control or an additional experiment would remove an alternative explanation.

model.label: Question
model.text: Is HSF1 needed for the full HSP70 response to heat shock in these cells?

model.label: Changed
model.text: HSF1-targeting siRNA versus scrambled siRNA or mock treatment; heat-shock status also has baseline comparisons.

model.label: Measured
model.text: HSF1 and HSP70 mRNA by normalized RT-qPCR and protein by normalized Western blot.

model.label: Comparison
model.text: Scrambled siRNA addresses nonspecific RNA/transfection effects; mock, no-heat-shock samples, GAPDH, and beta-actin address additional comparisons and normalization.

model.label: Evidence
model.text: HSF1 knockdown accompanies reduced HSP70 induction: HSP70 mRNA is 0.22 relative to mock in the heat-shock comparison.

model.label: Limit
model.text: Off-target effects, reference stability, detection range, and one cell line limit inference. Independent targeting sequences and a suitable rescue would strengthen attribution to HSF1.

coaches.title: Encoding Depth and Word Recall
coaches.focus: Design, evidence, and the limit of a claim
prompts: State the research question. Name what changed, what was measured, and what was held constant.
Select the data comparison that matters. Describe its direction before calculating.
State one conclusion and one thing this design cannot establish.
hints: Treat each column as a variable with units. Identify which comparisons isolate the proposed factor.
A result supports a claim only within this design. Ask whether a control or an additional experiment would remove an alternative explanation.

model.label: Question
model.text: Does encoding task affect later free recall?

model.label: Changed
model.text: Randomly assigned structural, phonological, semantic, or self-reference encoding task.

model.label: Measured
model.text: Number of words correctly recalled out of 60.

model.label: Comparison
model.text: Shallow-processing tasks provide comparison conditions; word exposure time, filler delay, and recall time are matched, with a blinded scorer.

model.label: Evidence
model.text: Mean recall is 27.4 for self-reference and 21.8 for semantic processing, versus 9.2 and 11.5 for the shallow tasks. The rounded summaries give F approximately 102.8; use the reported post-hoc comparisons to identify differing pairs.

model.label: Limit
model.text: Means alone do not establish significance. Undergraduates recalling words after a short delay do not establish effects for every population or study task.

science.stem: A reaction is measured at 0, 2, and 4 minutes. Product concentrations are 2, 6, and 10 μM. Which observation is supported?
options: The interval rate is 2 μM/min in both intervals.
The enzyme must be inhibited during the second interval.
The reaction has reached equilibrium at 4 minutes.
science.explanation: Each two-minute interval adds 4 μM, giving a slope of 2 μM/min. Neither inhibition nor equilibrium follows from these data.

psychSoc.stem: Groups A and B recalled means of 12 and 16 words. No variability, sample size, or significance test is reported. Which statement follows?
options: B has the higher observed mean, but statistical significance is undetermined.
Every person in B recalled more words than every person in A.
The intervention caused the difference even without a study design.
psychSoc.explanation: The reported means establish a descriptive difference only. Variability and design information are needed for stronger inferences.

cars.stem: An author argues: “Museums can broaden access to art, but lower admission fees alone do not remove every barrier.” Which claim best preserves that qualification?
options: Admission fees are the only barrier to art.
Lower fees may help, while other obstacles can remain.
All barriers disappear when admission is free.
cars.explanation: The author allows a benefit while limiting its sufficiency. The other choices remove or reverse that qualification.

carsTransfer.stem: A writer favors trying new policies when they can be reversed and their effects monitored. Which case best applies both conditions?
options: Demolishing a building permanently without collecting outcome data.
Keeping every existing policy forever because change has costs.
Calling an irreversible decision an experiment after it fails.
Testing adjustable library hours for a month and tracking attendance.
carsTransfer.explanation: Adjustable hours are reversible, and attendance provides an observable outcome. The other choices drop the stated conditions or replace the writer’s position.
